# JusPrin Agent UI

The local React/TypeScript application that renders the Agent conversation
pane inside `wxWebView`. It talks to OrcaSlicer exclusively through the
versioned `jusprin-agent-bridge` JSON protocol whose shared source of truth is
`resources/jusprin/agent/protocol.json`; the native side lives in
`src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/`.

The page renders native state and submits typed requests. It never owns an
editable copy of the project or conversation: the native `AgentHost` is
authoritative, and every reload re-runs the handshake and reconstructs the
page from the host's `state` message.

## Building

CMake builds this page whenever an input changes (`npm ci` from the lockfile, then `npm run build`). The output is `resources/jusprin/agent/index.html`; it is generated, not committed. Node/npm is required unless you configure with `-DJUSPRIN_BUILD_WEB=OFF` and supply that file yourself.

```bash
cmake --build build/arm64 --config RelWithDebInfo --target jusprin_web
```

The bundle must stay a single self-contained file (`vite-plugin-singlefile`):
WKWebView does not reliably load `file:` subresources.

To point the running app at a Vite dev server instead of the packaged file (hot
module reload):

```bash
cd src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI && npm run dev
JUSPRIN_AGENT_DEV_URL=http://localhost:5173 ./build/arm64/src/OrcaSlicer.app/Contents/MacOS/OrcaSlicer
```

Adjust the binary path for your build tree and platform. The environment
variable is read once at construction; there is no settings UI for it.

## Testing

```bash
npm test        # vitest: protocol, bridge client, reducer, and DOM interaction tests
```

The deterministic conversation scenarios (`/fail`, `/flaky`, `/slow`) are
implemented natively in `DeterministicMockAgent.cpp` and asserted by
`tests/agent/test_agent_bridge.cpp`; the tests here exercise the page against
a scripted mock host playing the same protocol.

### State matrices

`src/visual/` holds one state input per state on the Figma page **Agent UI ·
States & Components**: runtime and header states, chat
list, composer, messages, manufacturing history, the earlier-chat notice, and
the printer chat. Each is rendered by the production components, or by the
real `App` against a scripted host, so a state is covered only if real inputs
can produce it. `npm test` asserts every one renders; with an output path the
same test writes a review page of all of them at the 429 and 320 DIP dock
widths in both appearances:

```bash
PREVIEW_OUT=/tmp/agent-ui-states.html npx vitest run AgentUiStateMatrix
```

Open the page with `?show=<case>,<case>&mode=dark&dock=320` to narrow it to
the states being compared with a Figma node. The page proves rendering only;
look at the running app as well (`tests/shell`'s capture modes write PNGs of
the real WebView).

## Design

`tokens.ts` imports `resources/jusprin/ui/design-tokens.json` at build time
and writes it onto the root element as custom properties: `--<group>-<name>`
for the semantic colors of the appearance the host reports, and, once at
startup, `--radius-<name>` for each radius plus `--font-<role>` holding the
complete `font` shorthand of each type role and `--font-code` for the one
monospace role, used only for code, keys, paths and IDs. `styles.css` may use only those variables for
color, radius, and type, and only the spacing scale (4 through 48) for
padding, margin, and gap; `styles.test.ts` reads the stylesheet from disk and
fails on any literal outside that contract, naming the offending line.

editable copy of the project or conversation: the native `AgentHost` is
authoritative, and every reload re-runs the handshake and reconstructs the
page from the host's `state` message.

## Building

CMake builds this page whenever an input changes (`npm ci` from the lockfile, then `npm run build`). The output is `resources/jusprin/agent/index.html`; it is generated, not committed. Node/npm is required unless you configure with `-DJUSPRIN_BUILD_WEB=OFF` and supply that file yourself.

```bash
cmake --build build/arm64 --config RelWithDebInfo --target jusprin_web
```

The bundle must stay a single self-contained file (`vite-plugin-singlefile`):
WKWebView does not reliably load `file:` subresources.

To point the running app at a Vite dev server instead of the packaged file (hot
module reload):

```bash
cd src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI && npm run dev
JUSPRIN_AGENT_DEV_URL=http://localhost:5173 ./build/arm64/src/OrcaSlicer.app/Contents/MacOS/OrcaSlicer
```

Adjust the binary path for your build tree and platform. The environment
variable is read once at construction; there is no settings UI for it.

## Testing

```bash
npm test        # vitest: protocol, bridge client, reducer, and DOM interaction tests
```

The deterministic conversation scenarios (`/fail`, `/flaky`, `/slow`) are
implemented natively in `DeterministicMockAgent.cpp` and asserted by
`tests/agent/test_agent_bridge.cpp`; the tests here exercise the page against
a scripted mock host playing the same protocol.

### State matrices

`src/visual/` holds one state input per state on the Figma page **Agent UI ·
States & Components**: runtime and header states, chat
list, composer, messages, manufacturing history, the earlier-chat notice, and
the printer chat. Each is rendered by the production components, or by the
real `App` against a scripted host, so a state is covered only if real inputs
can produce it. `npm test` asserts every one renders; with an output path the
same test writes a review page of all of them at the 429 and 320 DIP dock
widths in both appearances:

```bash
PREVIEW_OUT=/tmp/agent-ui-states.html npx vitest run AgentUiStateMatrix
```

Open the page with `?show=<case>,<case>&mode=dark&dock=320` to narrow it to
the states being compared with a Figma node. The page proves rendering only;
look at the running app as well (`tests/shell`'s capture modes write PNGs of
the real WebView).

## Design

`tokens.ts` imports `resources/jusprin/ui/design-tokens.json` at build time
and writes it onto the root element as custom properties: `--<group>-<name>`
for the semantic colors of the appearance the host reports, and, once at
startup, `--radius-<name>` for each radius plus `--font-<role>` holding the
complete `font` shorthand of each type role and `--font-code` for the one
monospace role, used only for code, keys, paths and IDs. `styles.css` may use only those variables for
color, radius, and type, and only the spacing scale (4 through 48) for
padding, margin, and gap; `styles.test.ts` reads the stylesheet from disk and
fails on any literal outside that contract, naming the offending line.

<result>I've mapped the host side. The main finding: there is no separate settings-reader class. The one reader underneath every tool is the `IWorkspace` interface, implemented by `OrcaWorkspaceAdapter`, plus a few header-only helpers. That reader only covers four scopes (process, object, filament preset, printer preset).

All paths below are relative to `/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/.claude/worktrees/sharp-snyder-2d935e`.

## 1. The six tools

**Where they live**
- **Schemas:** `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ToolRegistry.cpp`, built in one `definitions{...}` vector.
- **Dispatch:** `ToolExecutionCoordinator::execute()` in `Agent/ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp`, branching on `ToolHandler::*`.
- **JSON shaping:** `Agent/ToolResults.cpp`.
- **MCP:** uses the same coordinator. `Mcp/McpRuntime.cpp:71` calls `m_coordinator.submit(...)`.

**Common pieces**
- **Scope enum** (`ToolRegistry.cpp:946`): `"process" | "object" | "filament" | "printer"`.
- **`target`** (`:950`): `{objectId?, preset?}`. Leave it out for process; object takes `objectId`; filament and printer take the preset's exact name.
- **Parsing:** `settings_target()` at `ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp:318-340` maps the strings to `Workspace::SettingsScope`.
- **Every settings result also carries** `scope, presetName, sessionId, revision, truncated` (`settings_output` at `ToolRegistry.cpp:926-934`, filled by `settings_context` at `ToolResults.cpp:40-45`).

**The tools**

| Tool | Schema | Handler | Workspace call | JSON builder |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `settings_search` | `ToolRegistry.cpp:1039-1045` | `ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp:1891-1914` | `search_settings(SettingsQuery)` | `settings_search_result`, `ToolResults.cpp:82-104` |
| `settings_get` | `:1046-1055` | `:1916-1932` | `read_settings(keys, target)` | `settings_read_result`, `:106-126` |
| `settings_preview_patch` | `:1056-1061` | `:1934-1950` | `preview_settings(SettingsPatch)` | `settings_preview_result`, `:128-140` |
| `settings_apply_patch` | `:1062-1070` | preflight `:747-770`, run `:1952-1983` | `apply_settings(patch, expected, applied)` | `settings_apply_result`, `:142-162` |
| `presets_list` | `:1396-1409` | `:1678-1692` | `list_presets(PresetQuery)` | `presets_list_result`, `:898-909` |
| `workspace_inspect` | `:1484-1512` | `:956-1003` | `snapshot()`, plus product state | `workspace_inspection`, `:752-795`, plus section builders |

**Inputs and outputs**
- **`settings_search`**
  - In: `{scope, target?, query, limit 1..25, cursor, writable, changedOnly}`. `scope` and `query` are required.
  - Out: `{items:[{key, type, label, category, description, unit, min?, max?, enumValues[], enumLabels[], writable, truncated}], nextCursor}`.
  - The cursor format is `"offset:N"`.
- **`settings_get`**
  - In: `{scope, target?, keys[1..32]}`.
  - Out: `{items:[{key, value, type, label, unit, differsFromPreset, differsFromSystem, writable, overridden?}], unknownKeys:[issue]}`.
  - `value` is Orca's `ConfigOption::serialize()` string.
  - `get` returns no `category`, enum options or preset value; only `search` returns those definition fields.
  - `overridden` appears only for object scope.
- **`settings_preview_patch`**
  - In: `{scope, target?, changes:{key: string|number|bool} (1..32), persistAs?}`.
  - Out: `{valid, changes:[{key, before, after}], dependencies:[...], issues:[issue], warnings:[issue]}`.
  - Issue shape: `{key, code, message, allowed[], suggestions[], min?, max?, truncated}`.
- **`settings_apply_patch`**
  - In: the preview inputs plus `expectedSessionId, expectedRevision`.
  - Out: `{applied, changes, normalized[], savedAs, presetDirty, projectUndo}`. `projectUndo` is true only for object scope.
  - Preflight re-runs the preview and stashes `previewedChanges` into the arguments (`:765-768`).
  - The revision check is `settings_revision_holds` (`:52-58`).
- **`presets_list`**
  - In: `{kind: printer|filament|process, query, compatibleOnly (default true), limit, cursor}`.
  - Out: `{items:[{name, label, vendor, system, selected, compatible}], total, nextCursor, truncated, sessionId, revision}`.
- **`workspace_inspect`**
  - In: `{sections:[summary|project|objects|intent|plan|slicing|printer|activities]}`.
  - Summary (`ToolResults.cpp:784-792`): `projectName, projectDirty, printerPreset, filamentPreset, activePlateId, plateCount, objectCount, plates{items:[{plateId, name, active, sliced, objectCount, objects}]}, selection, history`.
  - The objects section (`ToolResults.cpp:592-609`) has `overrideCount` per object.
  - Its own description says it exposes no setting values.

**How scope works**

`OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:2725-2756` decides which config is read:
- **Process:** the selected print preset's edited copy.
- **Object:** the same process config with `ModelObject::config` layered on top. Overridable keys are `PrintRegionConfig` or `PrintObjectConfig` options (`OrcaSettingDefinitions.hpp:53-58`).
- **Filament or printer:** the preset looked up by name. If it is the selected one, its edited copy is read; otherwise it is read as saved.
- **Filament slots:** there is no slot index in this API. The slot list is `preset_bundle->filament_presets` (see `filament_slot()` at `:2801`).
- **Not supported by any settings tool:** plate, part, modifier, layer range.
  - Those are only summarised read-only in `applied_setup_of()` (`OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:228-309`). It walks object config, `layer_config_ranges`, each volume's config and painting, and emits `SetupLocalOverride{target, kind, key, value, label, display}`.
  - The kinds it emits: `"object"`, `"height range"`, `"modifier"`, `"part"`, `"support blocker"`, `"support enforcer"`, `"negative part"`, plus paint artifacts.
- **Which keys a scope holds:** `scope_options()` → `Preset::print_options()`, `filament_options()` or `printer_options()` (`OrcaSettingDefinitions.hpp:61-81`).

**How "changed from preset" is computed** (`read_settings`, `OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:2914-2963`):
```cpp
if (owner.selected) {
    dirty  = owner.collection->current_dirty_options();
    system = owner.collection->current_different_from_parent_options();
} else if (const Preset* base = owner.collection->get_preset_base(*owner.preset); ...)
    system = PresetCollection::dirty_options(owner.preset, base);
```
- `differsFromPreset` is set when the key is in `dirty`. `differsFromSystem` is set when it is in `system`.
- **Search's `changedOnly`** (`:2894-2899`) uses `object->config.keys()` for object scope, otherwise `current_dirty_options()`.
- **The setup card's deltas** (`snapshot()`, `:894-905`) use `prints.current_dirty_options()`, plus `current_dirty_options(true)` for filaments and printers. Each is fed to `preset_deltas_of()` (`:184-226`), which compares `get_edited_preset().config` against `get_selected_preset().config` per key.

None of these paths use a raw `DynamicPrintConfig::diff` for "changed". `diff` only appears in preview/apply, for predicting normalised dependencies (`:3022`, `:3141`).

## 2. The shared reader underneath

**Interface:** `Workspace::IWorkspace` (`Workspace/Workspace.hpp:1681`). The implementation is `Workspace::OrcaWorkspaceAdapter` (`Workspace/OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.hpp:63-69`), created in `Shell/ShellController.cpp:255`. Its public functions, all GUI-thread only:
```cpp
PresetListResult     list_presets(const PresetQuery&) const;                 // Workspace.hpp:1765
SettingsSearchResult search_settings(const SettingsQuery&) const;            // :1771
SettingsReadResult   read_settings(const std::vector<std::string>& keys, const SettingsTarget& = {}) const; // :1772
SettingsPreview      preview_settings(const SettingsPatch&) const;           // :1773
CommandResult        apply_settings(const SettingsPatch&, const std::vector<SettingChange>& expected, SettingsPreview& applied); // :1774
WorkspaceSnapshot    snapshot() const;   // carries preset_deltas and applied_setup (Workspace.hpp:317-319)
```

**Value types** (`Workspace.hpp:1592-1679`): `SettingDefinition{key, type, label, category, description, unit, min, max, enum_values, enum_labels, writable}`, `SettingValue`, `SettingsScope`, `SettingsTarget`, `SettingsQuery`, and the related result structs.

**Header-only helpers** that don't need the GUI:
- `Workspace/OrcaSettingDefinitions.hpp`:
  - `setting_type()` `:13`
  - `setting_definition(key)` `:35`
  - `object_setting()` `:53`
  - `scope_options()` `:61`
  - `has_scope_setting()` `:68`
  - `scope_definitions(scope)` `:75`: every definition in a scope
- `Workspace/SettingsSupport.hpp`:
  - `blocked_setting()` and `writable_setting()` `:20-48`
  - `withheld_setting()` `:61`: print-host credentials, which must never be returned
  - `scope_name()` `:72`
  - `search_setting_definitions()` `:94`
- `Workspace/SettingDisplay.hpp`: `unit_of()` `:59`, `display_value()` `:94`, `display_change()` `:128`.

Two helpers are private to `OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp` and can't be called from outside: `preset_deltas_of()`, which is the only code that attaches the Orca tab page and group, and `applied_setup_of()`.

**Limits a direct caller inherits:** `read_settings` takes at most 32 keys (`:2918`) and search pages at most 25. There is no "read every value in a scope" call. Iterating `scope_definitions()` in batches of 32 is the existing building block.

## 3. The bridge (page-initiated requests)

**Transport**
- The page posts with `window.wx.postMessage(JSON)` (`WebShared/bridgeClient.ts:58-63`, `post()` at `:149-159`). Page ids are `w-N`.
- The host delivers back through `window.__jusprinBridge.deliver(...)` (`Agent/AgentWebView.cpp:167-174`).
- Incoming messages go `on_script_message` → `AgentHost::on_page_message` (`AgentWebView.cpp:203`, `AgentHost.cpp:975`) → `dispatch_page_message` (`AgentHost.cpp:998-1093`). That function is an if/else chain on `type`.
- Anything the chain doesn't know falls to `m_page_message_handler(type, payload)` (`:1091`). If that returns false, the host sends `bridge_error` `unknown_type`.

**Responses**
- `send_envelope(type, payload, correlation_id)` (`AgentHost.cpp:804-833`) builds `{protocol, version, id:"h-N", type, sessionId, revision, payload, correlationId?}`.
- Handlers answer with `correlation_id = envelope_id`, i.e. the page's `w-N`.
- The public `send_page_envelope(type, payload)` (`:2336`) sends no correlation id.

**Capabilities**
- The host's list is `Protocol::capabilities()` in `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/AgentProtocol.hpp:25-36`. Message-type constants are in the same file (`:39-124`).
- It must match `resources/jusprin/agent/protocol.json` (`capabilities`, `pageMessageTypes`, `hostMessageTypes`). That is enforced by `tests/agent/test_agent_bridge.cpp:322-349` and `AgentUI/src/bridge/protocol.test.ts`.
- The page imports the same JSON (`protocol.ts:6-10`) and sends it in `hello` (`bridgeClient.ts:132-135`).
- The host replies `hello_ack {version, capabilities, agent, appearance}` (`AgentHost.cpp:1267-1279`), then a full `state`.
- The page stores `hostCapabilities` (`state/store.ts:161-170`) and gates on it, e.g. `App.tsx:263`.

**A worked example: `mcp_catalog`**
1. Page sends it: `App.tsx:545`, `onRefresh={() => client.send('mcp_catalog', {})}`.
2. Types are declared in both unions in `protocol.ts:30` (page) and `:62` (host), with the payload type `McpCatalogPayload` at `:276-281`.
3. Host constant: `AgentProtocol.hpp:57`, `kMcpCatalog = "mcp_catalog"`.
4. Dispatch: `AgentHost.cpp:1060-1061` → `handle_mcp_catalog(envelope_id)` (`:3202-3226`). It builds the payload and ends with `send_envelope(Protocol::kMcpCatalog, payload.dump(), envelope_id)`.
5. Page reducer: `state/store.ts:230-231`, `case 'mcp_catalog': return {...state, mcpCatalog: envelope.payload}`.
6. Both lists in `resources/jusprin/agent/protocol.json` include `"mcp_catalog"`.

**The other hook:** `Shell/ShellController.cpp:345-375` registers `set_page_message_handler` for `shell_action`. It has direct `m_workspace` access (for example `compute_setup_estimates` calls `m_workspace->snapshot()` and `start_slice`), but it gets no envelope id to correlate a reply.

## 4. Where the setup card's data comes from

- **Builder:** `context_json(snapshot, configured, printer_review)` (`AgentHost.cpp:530-637`). It turns `snapshot.preset_deltas` into `presetDeltas:[{key, label, preset, value, presetType?, presetName?, display?, page?, group?}]` (`:572-582`). It turns `snapshot.applied_setup` into `appliedSetup{version, plateId, printableObjects, spiralMode, variableLayerHeight, objects, localOverrides[]}` (`:593-609`).
- **Chat fields:** `card_context()` (`:642-647`) adds `setupIntent` and `planHeadline` from the chat document. `setup_record` writes those.
- **Delivery:** the result travels as `state.payload.context` (`send_state`, `:941-943`) and as the `context` message (`send_context`, `:955-966`). `send_context` fires on workspace changes (`:682`, `:727`). A saved chat's copy is `chatResume.summary` (`:861`).
- **Page types:** `WorkspaceContext` and `PresetDeltaInfo` in `protocol.ts:317-431`. The reducer cases are `store.ts:174-` and `:210-211`.
- **Rendering:** `App.tsx:454-479` passes `cardContext` to `<SetupCard>`.
  - `SetupCard.tsx` doesn't count the deltas. It shows `overrideObjectCount` (`:162-165`) and a "View setup" link (`:332`).
  - The count text is on the setup page: `SetupPage.tsx:67`, `` `Changed from presets · ${deltas.length}` ``, grouped by `page · group` (`:59-90`, `:222`).

## 5. Category and label sources

- **`jusprin_catalogs` has nothing to do with settings.** It only builds translation `.mo` files with the product name substituted (`Brand/catalogs.cmake`, `Brand/brand_catalogs.py`). There is no settings-category JSON under `resources/jusprin/`; that folder holds `agent/protocol.json`, `home/protocol.json`, UI tokens and branding.
- **Source A: libslic3r's `ConfigOptionDef`.** `setting_definition()` uses `def.category`, `full_label`/`label`, `tooltip`, `sidetext` (unit) and `enum_values`/`enum_labels` (`OrcaSettingDefinitions.hpp:38-39`). This is the `category` that `settings_search` returns.
  - In `src/libslic3r/PrintConfig.cpp`, only 333 of 870 `this->add(` entries set a category.
  - The values: Quality 95, Support 59, Strength 48, Speed 42, empty 34, Advanced 20, Others 12, Machine limits 10, Extruders 8, Flush options 3, Other 1, Layers and Perimeters 1.
  - So it is partial and not the same as the tab layout.
- **Source B: Orca's actual tab page and group**, which do match the Quality / Strength / Speed / Support / Others tabs. It comes from `Search::OptionsSearcher::get_group_and_category(index_key)` (`src/slic3r/GUI/Search.hpp:137`), where the key is `"<Preset::Type>;<opt_key>"` with a `#0` fallback (`OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:175-178`, `:210-214`).
  - The searcher comes from `m_plater.sidebar().get_searcher()` (`:894`).
  - Today this is used only inside `preset_deltas_of()`, so only changed settings get a `page`/`group`. Neither `settings_search` nor `settings_get` exposes it.
  - The comment at `:206-209` says every option group registers here as its tab is built, in any user mode. The `PresetDelta` comment (`Workspace.hpp:224-225`) instead says page and group are empty when the search index lacks the setting in the current user mode.</result>

```cpp
if (owner.selected) {
```

questions.question: Should the first version of the All settings panel be read-only, or read-only plus the two actions the object board draws ("Use project value" on an object's own setting, and "Remove" on a support blocker)?

options.label: Read-only first (Recommended)
options.description: The panel only shows settings. The two actions come in a follow-up. This keeps this change to one new host read request plus the page; the actions need new host code that removes a key from an object's, part's or height range's config, deletes a blocker volume, takes an Orca undo snapshot, and writes a change-log entry, each needing its own tests.

options.label: Read-only plus the two actions
options.description: Both actions ship now. Roughly doubles the host work and the live testing, and the panel will reach you later. Edits beyond those two (changing a value) stay out either way; those go through the chat.

questions.question: With two or three filament slots the Filament group shows one column per slot. What should it do with four or more slots, where columns no longer fit in a 320 to 429 pixel pane?

options.label: Slot picker, one column (Recommended)
options.description: Above four slots the columns are replaced by a Select listing the slots (swatch, slot number, material); the group shows one slot at a time, starting with slot 1. Same rows as the column layout, so nothing is lost, and it needs no horizontal scrolling.

options.label: First three columns plus a picker
options.description: Keep three columns and add a Select to swap which three slots are shown. Denser, but the picker then means "which window of slots", which is harder to explain.

options.label: Always a picker
options.description: Never draw columns, even with two or three slots. Simplest to build, but it drops the side-by-side view the filaments board was drawn for.

questions.question: The Showing menu lists "Whole project" and each object. How should plates appear in it? An OrcaSlicer plate owns only eight settings (bed type, print sequence, first and other layer filament order, spiral vase, skirt angle, filament map), and everything else comes from the presets.

options.label: Plates as rows when there are 2+ (Recommended)
options.description: "Whole project" means the plate the canvas shows, as the setup card already does. With more than one plate, each plate is also a row in Showing; choosing one shows that plate's own settings ("same as project" for the rest) and the objects on it, like the object view does. With one plate no plate row is shown, and its own settings appear only in the presets box, as the project board draws.

options.label: Always list every plate
options.description: Each plate is a row even when there is only one. Consistent, but a one-plate project then has a row that repeats what the presets box says.

options.label: No plates in Showing
options.description: Only Whole project and objects. A plate's own settings appear in the presets box of the project view. The brief asked for plates in Showing, so I would only do this if you have changed your mind.

content.thinking:
The grep for IWorkspace implementers came up empty, so there's probably a fake workspace used in tests I need to find differently. I'm weighing whether to add a pure virtual `settings_catalog()` method to IWorkspace, which would force every implementation including fakes to define it, versus giving it a default implementation to avoid breaking existing code.

I'm leaning toward a defaulted virtual with an empty catalog by default so fakes stay untouched, but I'll need to find the actual fake workspace used in agent host tests to make sure it can be configured with useful catalog data for new tests. Now I'm sketching the JSON payload structure for the settings catalog, covering printer, process, filament, plate, and per-object override data.

For filament rows with nullable overrides like retraction length or z-hop, I'm working out how to mark a row as inherited from the printer when the filament's own value is nil, and how to map the filament key back to its corresponding printer key and extruder index so I can show "inherited from printer" values correctly.

For the bed temperature row, I need the page to select the correct config key based on the plate's bed type (textured, hot, cool, engineering, supertack plates), since Orca stores a separate temperature key per bed type plus an initial-layer variant, and I need to match the catalog's bed type name to the right key.

I found the function that maps bed type to temp key, so the host can attribute those keys and the page just consumes them. For the filament group rows in multi-slot view, I'm weighing whether to show only the handful of key rows the design calls out (nozzle temp, first layer temp, bed, fan speed) versus all ~150 filament settings in column form grouped by Orca's filament pages like Filament and Cooling -- leaning toward showing everything since this is meant to be "All settings."

I'm deciding to just show every filament setting row with the three-slot columns, grouped by page sub-headings rather than reducing bed rows to only plate-specific keys, since that's simpler and more faithful; the changed-only filter will naturally narrow things down. At 320px width the three-column layout will be tight, so I'll use CSS grid with min widths and let labels wrap instead of trying to force everything onto one line. For a single-slot project the filament group just falls back to simple name/value rows like other groups, and process settings will follow the same page-grouped structure as Orca's Quality and Strength tabs.

Now I'm thinking through object scope: local overrides only apply to the active plate's objects since that's what `appliedSetup` covers, but the panel's object selector should really let someone browse objects across all plates. So the catalog needs to walk every plate's objects and track their overrides and plate membership, building a structure like `objects: [{id, name, plateId, overrides: [...]}]`, reusing a refactored version of the applied-setup helper to add local overrides per object.

To avoid duplicating logic between the two collector functions, I'll extract a shared helper that gathers local overrides for a given model object and index, used by both code paths. For objects with no overrides, I'll show a "same as project" summary line, and for the plate scope itself I'm identifying which plate-level config keys belong to the plate (bed type, print sequence, layer sequencing, spiral mode, skirt angle, filament-related settings) versus which are inherited.

For each present key I'm building a row showing the label and display value, pulling the comparable project-wide value for contrast, and surfacing a "set on this plate" badge when a plate overrides a setting like bed type. I'm also working out selection logic — showing an object's own settings when one object is selected, or a plate's own settings plus its objects when multiple plates exist — and estimating the payload size (roughly 450 object rows, 450 filament rows, 200 printer rows, all under 150KB) to decide when to fetch data, such as on panel open and selection changes.

Now I'm deciding where to build the catalog JSON: I'll keep the Workspace layer GUI-agnostic with plain structs (SettingsCatalog, CatalogSetting, CatalogPreset, CatalogPlate, CatalogObject) defined in Workspace.hpp, and handle the actual JSON conversion separately in AgentHost.cpp alongside the existing context JSON logic, exposing a settings_catalog() method on IWorkspace.

Since AgentHost already holds a reference to IWorkspace and calls snapshot() on it directly, I can have handle_settings_catalog simply call m_workspace.settings_catalog() without needing a separate provider abstraction. For testing, I'll extend the FakeWorkspace used in agent_bridge_tests with a settings_catalog_request test verifying the fake payload comes through, and update the existing protocol.json capability test to include the new type constants.

Now thinking through the AllSettingsPanel component itself - I need a header with back button and title, a Showing select, search, a segmented control, and a body organized by scope. For the generic Select component, I'm considering reusing the existing chat-menu popover styling rather than inventing new classes, so I'm looking at how ChatNavigation builds its menu to see if there's an existing ActionMenu pattern I can reuse instead of duplicating popover logic.

I want to check ModelPickers.tsx since it combines a picker with menu and search, making it the closest existing analog to the Select I need. I also need to trace how printer identity data flows through the app - bed temperature keys in Orca, PartPlate config access, filament colour and material sourcing, and nozzle info - so I can reuse the same setupIdentity logic for populating these selects.

Actually, the presets box is simpler than I thought: context already exposes setupIdentity with printer, nozzles, plateType, and filaments (each with preset and material), plus context.printer.process and presetDeltas giving counts per preset type. So I can build the presets box directly from context, pulling swatch colours from the catalog rather than fetching anything new.

entries.name: SendMessage
entries.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

# CLAUDE.md - Testing Guide for OrcaSlicer

This guide provides comprehensive instructions for Claude Code when writing, maintaining, and understanding tests in the OrcaSlicer codebase.

## ⚠️ CRITICAL RULES - MUST FOLLOW

### 1. **SECTIONS IN LOOPS - NEVER REUSE NAMES**
❌ **WRONG**: Will cause unpredictable behavior
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Bad loop sections") {
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) {
        SECTION("Same name") {  // WRONG! Same name used multiple times
            REQUIRE(i >= 0);
        }
    }
}
```

✅ **CORRECT**: Use DYNAMIC_SECTION or incorporate counter
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Good loop sections") {
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) {
        DYNAMIC_SECTION("Section " << i) {  // Unique name per iteration
            REQUIRE(i >= 0);
        }
    }
}
```

### 2. **THREAD SAFETY - ASSERTIONS ARE NOT THREAD-SAFE**
❌ **WRONG**: Will cause undefined behavior or crashes
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Multi-threaded test") {
    std::vector<std::thread> threads;
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) {
        threads.emplace_back([]() {
            REQUIRE(some_calculation() == expected);  // NOT THREAD-SAFE!
        });
    }
}
```

✅ **CORRECT**: Synchronize results, test on main thread
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Multi-threaded test") {
    std::vector<std::thread> threads;
    std::atomic<int> passed{0};
    
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) {
        threads.emplace_back([&passed]() {
            if (some_calculation() == expected) {
                passed++;
            }
        });
    }
    
    for (auto& t : threads) t.join();
    REQUIRE(passed == 4);  // Test results on main thread
}
```

### 3. **EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION - AVOID BINARY OPERATORS**
❌ **WRONG**: Cannot decompose properly
```cpp
REQUIRE(a > 0 && b < 10);  // Shows "false" on failure, not individual values
```

✅ **CORRECT**: Split into separate assertions
```cpp
REQUIRE(a > 0);
REQUIRE(b < 10);  // Each shows individual values on failure
```

### 4. **FLOATING POINT - NEVER USE APPROX**
❌ **WRONG**: Approx is deprecated and asymmetric
```cpp
REQUIRE(calculated_value == Catch::Approx(expected));  // Deprecated!
```

✅ **CORRECT**: Use floating point matchers
```cpp
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_value, WithinAbs(expected, 0.001));
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_value, WithinRel(expected, 0.01));  // 1% tolerance
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_value, WithinULP(expected, 4));     // 4 ULPs apart
```

### 5. **TEST ORDERING - ALWAYS USE RANDOM ORDER**
✅ **REQUIRED**: For CI/CD and development
```bash
# Essential flags for running tests
./tests --order rand --warn NoAssertions

# For test sharding (parallel execution), share random seed
./tests --order rand --shard-index 0 --shard-count 3 --rng-seed 0xBEEF
./tests --order rand --shard-index 1 --shard-count 3 --rng-seed 0xBEEF
./tests --order rand --shard-index 2 --shard-count 3 --rng-seed 0xBEEF
```

## Overview of OrcaSlicer's Testing Framework

OrcaSlicer uses **Catch2 v3** (currently v3.11.0, vendored in `tests/catch2/`) as its primary testing framework. The test suite is organized into several modules that mirror the project's architectural components:

> **Note**: Test files include the framework via `#include <catch2/catch_all.hpp>` (the v3 single-header convenience include). All v3 features described in this guide are available.

### Test Structure
```
tests/
├── CMakeLists.txt              # Main test configuration
├── catch_main.hpp              # Custom test reporter
├── libslic3r/                  # Core library tests (21 test files)
├── fff_print/                  # FFF printing tests (12 test files)
├── sla_print/                  # SLA printing tests (4 test files)
├── libnest2d/                  # 2D nesting tests
├── slic3rutils/               # Utility tests
├── data/                      # Test data files and meshes
└── catch2/                    # Catch2 framework files
```

### Build Integration
- Tests are built using CMake with `catch_discover_tests()` integration
- Each test module creates a separate executable (e.g., `libslic3r_tests`, `fff_print_tests`)
- Test data directory is available via `TEST_DATA_DIR` preprocessor definition
- Custom verbose console reporter provides detailed test output

## Test Suite Organization

### libslic3r Tests
Core slicing engine tests covering:
- **Geometry operations**: Points, polygons, lines, Voronoi diagrams
- **File formats**: STL, 3MF, AMF parsing and validation
- **Algorithms**: Clipper operations, mesh boolean operations, optimization
- **Configuration**: Print settings validation and parsing
- **Utilities**: String processing, time utilities, data structures

### fff_print Tests
Fused Filament Fabrication specific tests:
- **G-code generation**: Writer functionality, cooling, lift/unlift
- **Slicing algorithms**: Layer generation, infill patterns
- **Print mechanics**: Flow calculations, extrusion, support material
- **Model processing**: Print objects, skirt/brim generation

### sla_print Tests
Stereolithography specific tests:
- **SLA print processing**: Layer curing, support generation
- **Raycast operations**: Light path calculations
- **Test utilities**: SLA-specific helper functions

## Writing New Tests - Best Practices

### File Organization
1. **Naming Convention**: `test_<feature>.cpp` (e.g., `test_geometry.cpp`)
2. **Header Structure**: Include `<catch2/catch_all.hpp>` first, then relevant headers
3. **Namespace Usage**: Use `using namespace Slic3r;` for convenience
4. **File Placement**: Add to appropriate test directory and update CMakeLists.txt

### Test Naming and Structure
```cpp
#include <catch2/catch_all.hpp>
#include "libslic3r/Point.hpp"

using namespace Slic3r;

TEST_CASE("Feature description", "[category_tag]") {
    // Test implementation
}
```

### Tagging System
Use descriptive tags for test categorization:
- `[Geometry]` - Geometric operations and calculations
- `[GCodeWriter]` - G-code generation functionality  
- `[Config]` - Configuration and settings tests
- `[FileFormat]` - File I/O operations (STL, 3MF, etc.)
- `[Algorithm]` - Core algorithms and processing
- `[Performance]` - Performance benchmarks (if applicable)

## Catch2 Features Guide

### Basic Assertions
```cpp
// Primary assertions - stop test on failure
REQUIRE(expression);
REQUIRE_FALSE(expression);

// Continuing assertions - continue test after failure  
CHECK(expression);
CHECK_FALSE(expression);

// Non-failing checks - record result but don't fail test
CHECK_NOFAIL(expression);  // Useful for assumptions that might be violated
```

### Exception Testing
```cpp
// Verify no exception is thrown
REQUIRE_NOTHROW(function_call());

// Verify any exception is thrown
REQUIRE_THROWS(risky_function());

// Verify specific exception type
REQUIRE_THROWS_AS(function_call(), SpecificException);

// Verify exception message
REQUIRE_THROWS_WITH(function_call(), "Expected error message");

// Verify exception with matchers (for partial matching)
REQUIRE_THROWS_MATCHES(function_call(), SpecificException, 
                       Catch::Matchers::Message("contains this"));
```

### Complex Assertions with Matchers
```cpp
#include <catch2/matchers/catch_matchers.hpp>

// String matchers
using Catch::Matchers::StartsWith;
using Catch::Matchers::EndsWith;
using Catch::Matchers::ContainsSubstring;
using Catch::Matchers::Equals;
using Catch::Matchers::Matches;  // Regex matching

REQUIRE_THAT(result_string, StartsWith("Expected prefix"));
REQUIRE_THAT(result_string, ContainsSubstring("middle part"));
REQUIRE_THAT(result_string, Matches(".*pattern.*"));

// Floating point matchers - ALWAYS use these instead of Approx!
using Catch::Matchers::WithinAbs;
using Catch::Matchers::WithinRel;
using Catch::Matchers::WithinULP;

REQUIRE_THAT(float_value, WithinAbs(expected, 0.001));     // Absolute tolerance
REQUIRE_THAT(float_value, WithinRel(expected, 0.01));      // Relative tolerance (1%)
REQUIRE_THAT(float_value, WithinULP(expected, 4));         // ULP difference (requires IEEE-754)

// Combining matchers
REQUIRE_THAT(value, WithinRel(expected, 0.001) || WithinAbs(0.0, 0.000001));
```

### Sections for Test Organization
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Complex feature testing", "[Feature]") {
    // Common setup code
    SomeObject obj;
    
    SECTION("First scenario") {
        // Specific test case
        REQUIRE(obj.method1() == expected_value);
    }
    
    SECTION("Second scenario") {
        // Another test case with same setup
        REQUIRE(obj.method2() == other_expected);
    }
}
```

### BDD-Style Tests
Use for complex scenarios and user story testing:

> **Note**: BDD macros are aliases for TEST_CASE and SECTION with prefixed names
```cpp
SCENARIO("User performs complex operation", "[UserStory]") {
    GIVEN("A specific setup condition") {
        GCodeWriter writer;
        // Setup code
        
        WHEN("User performs action") {
            auto result = writer.some_operation();
            
            THEN("Expected outcome occurs") {
                REQUIRE(result.size() > 0);
                
                AND_WHEN("Follow-up action occurs") {
                    auto next_result = writer.next_operation();
                    
                    THEN("Final outcome is correct") {
                        REQUIRE(next_result == expected);
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
```

### Data Generators for Parameterized Tests
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Function works with various inputs", "[Algorithm]") {
    auto test_value = GENERATE(1, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13);
    
    REQUIRE(is_odd(test_value));
    REQUIRE(test_value > 0);
}

// Range-based generators
TEST_CASE("Range testing", "[Algorithm]") {
    auto i = GENERATE(range(1, 10));  // 1 to 9
    REQUIRE(process_value(i) > i);
}

// Using variables in generators (requires GENERATE_COPY or GENERATE_REF)
TEST_CASE("Generator with variables", "[Algorithm]") {
    std::vector<int> values = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
    auto test_value = GENERATE_REF(from_range(values));  // Use GENERATE_REF for references
    
    REQUIRE(test_value > 0);
}

// Custom generators
TEST_CASE("Random values", "[Algorithm]") {
    auto random_int = GENERATE(take(100, random(-1000, 1000)));  // 100 random values
    REQUIRE(process_random_value(random_int));
}
```

### Test Fixtures
```cpp
class GeometryFixture {
public:
    Point origin{0, 0};
    Point unit_x{1, 0};
    Point unit_y{0, 1};
    
    mutable double tolerance = EPSILON;  // Use mutable for data that might change
};

// Standard fixture - new instance per test run
TEST_CASE_METHOD(GeometryFixture, "Point operations", "[Geometry]") {
    REQUIRE(origin.distance_to(unit_x) == 1.0);
}

// Persistent fixture - single instance for entire test case (v3.2.0+)
TEST_CASE_PERSISTENT_FIXTURE(GeometryFixture, "Persistent operations", "[Geometry]") {
    static int call_count = 0;
    ++call_count;
    INFO("This fixture persists across sections, call: " << call_count);

    }

    }

// Template fixtures for type-parameterized tests
template<typename T>
class NumericFixture {
public:
    T zero = T{0};

```

### Advanced Testing Features

#### Logging and Information Macros
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Advanced logging", "[Logging]") {
    INFO("This info persists until end of scope");
    
    SECTION("Section A") {
        INFO("Section A specific info");
        CAPTURE(some_variable, another_var);  // Captures variable names and values
        CHECK(some_condition);
    }
    
    SECTION("Section B") {
        UNSCOPED_INFO("This survives beyond its scope");  // v2.7.0+
        CHECK(other_condition);
    }
}

// Warning and explicit control
TEST_CASE("Explicit test control", "[Control]") {
    WARN("This warns but doesn't fail the test");
    
    if (precondition_not_met) {
        SKIP("Reason");  // Marks the test as skipped (v3.3.0+, available)
        return;
    }
    
    if (critical_failure) {
        FAIL("Critical condition failed");  // Fails and stops test
    }
    
    SUCCEED("Reached successful completion");  // Explicit success marker
}
```

#### Static Assertions (Compile-time Testing)

```cpp
TEST_CASE("Compile-time checks", "[Static]") {
    STATIC_REQUIRE(sizeof(int) >= 4);  // Checked at compile time
    STATIC_REQUIRE_FALSE(std::is_void_v<int>);
    
    // For traits and template metaprogramming

}
```

#### Conditional Testing

```cpp
TEST_CASE("Conditional blocks", "[Conditional]") {
    int value = get_test_value();
    
    // These record the expression but don't count as test failures (v3.0.1+)
    CHECKED_IF(value > 0) {
        // This block runs if value > 0
        REQUIRE(value <= 100);

        // This block runs if value <= 0

```

```bash
cd build && ./tests/libslic3r/libslic3r_tests --reporter compact     # Minimal output
```

```cpp
std::string config_path = std::string(TEST_DATA_DIR) + "/test_config/printer.ini";
```

## Common Pitfalls and Solutions

### Floating-Point Comparisons

> **CRITICAL**: Never use Approx - it's deprecated due to asymmetry and other issues

❌ **Incorrect**:
```cpp
REQUIRE(calculated_volume == expected_volume);           // Exact equality
REQUIRE(calculated_volume == Catch::Approx(expected));   // Deprecated! Asymmetric!
```

✅ **Correct**: Always use floating point matchers
```cpp
// Absolute tolerance - good when values are near zero
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, WithinAbs(expected_volume, 0.001));

// Relative tolerance - good for values with different magnitudes
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, WithinRel(expected_volume, 0.01));  // 1% tolerance

// ULP (Units in Last Place) - most precise, requires IEEE-754
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, WithinULP(expected_volume, 4));

// Combined approach - relative OR absolute
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, 
    WithinRel(expected_volume, 0.001) || WithinAbs(0.0, 0.000001));

// Precision control for output
Catch::StringMaker<double>::precision = 15;  // Show more decimal places
```

### Why Approx is Problematic:
- **Asymmetric**: `Approx(10).epsilon(0.1) != 11.1` but `Approx(11.1).epsilon(0.1) == 10`
- **Double-only**: All computation done in `double`, causes issues with `float` inputs  
- **Default behavior**: Only uses relative comparison, so `Approx(0) == X` only works for `X == 0`

### Path Handling
❌ **Incorrect**:
```cpp
std::string path = TEST_DATA_DIR + "/model.obj";  // May have path separator issues
```

✅ **Correct**:
```cpp
std::string path = std::string(TEST_DATA_DIR) + "/model.obj";
// or use boost::filesystem for complex path operations
```

### Exception Testing
❌ **Incorrect**:
```cpp
bool threw_exception = false;
try {
    risky_function();
} catch (...) {
    threw_exception = true;
}
REQUIRE(threw_exception);
```

✅ **Correct**:
```cpp
REQUIRE_THROWS(risky_function());
// or for specific exceptions
REQUIRE_THROWS_AS(risky_function(), SpecificException);
```

### Thread Safety

⚠️ **CRITICAL**: Catch2 assertions are **NOT thread-safe** by default!

> **Note**: Catch2 v3.9.0+ has opt-in thread-safe assertions via `CATCH_CONFIG_EXPERIMENTAL_THREAD_SAFE_ASSERTIONS`. OrcaSlicer is on v3.11.0 but does not enable this flag, so assertions remain non-thread-safe by default.

❌ **Incorrect**: Will cause undefined behavior or crashes
```cpp
std::thread t([&]() {
    REQUIRE(threaded_operation() == expected);  // NOT THREAD-SAFE!
    CHECK(other_operation());                   // NOT THREAD-SAFE!
});
```

✅ **Correct**: Collect results, assert on main thread
```cpp
std::atomic<bool> success{false};
std::atomic<int> error_count{0};

std::thread t([&]() {
    // Do work in thread, collect results
    bool result1 = (threaded_operation() == expected);
    bool result2 = other_operation();
    
    if (result1 && result2) {
        success = true;
    } else {
        error_count++;
    }
});

t.join();

// Assert results on main thread
REQUIRE(success);
REQUIRE(error_count == 0);
```

#### Thread Safety Rules:
- **REQUIRE family**: Would terminate process in spawned threads (throws exception with no try-catch)
- **CHECK family**: Not thread-safe, can corrupt internal state
- **SKIP, FAIL, SUCCEED**: Not thread-safe even with v3 thread-safe assertions
- **Message macros**: INFO, CAPTURE, WARN - not thread-safe
- **STATIC_REQUIRE/CHECK**: Not thread-safe (relies on runtime registration)

### Memory Management
Use RAII and smart pointers in tests:
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Resource management", "[Memory]") {
    auto model = std::make_unique<Model>();
    // Automatic cleanup on test completion/failure
    
    REQUIRE(model->objects.empty());
}
```

```cpp
// In CMakeLists.txt or as preprocessor definition
#define CATCH_CONFIG_FAST_COMPILE  // 20% faster compilation, disables some features

```

### Runtime Performance
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Performance-sensitive test", "[Performance]") {
    // Manual timing example (Catch2's built-in BENCHMARK macro is also available)
    auto start = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
    
    auto result = expensive_operation();
    
    auto end = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
    auto duration = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::milliseconds>(end - start);
    
    REQUIRE(result.is_valid());
    REQUIRE(duration.count() < 1000);  // Should complete in < 1 second
    
    INFO("Operation took " << duration.count() << "ms");
}
```

```cpp
// For Windows builds - detects memory leaks
#define CATCH_CONFIG_WINDOWS_CRTDBG  // Must be defined for whole build
```

## Integration with CMake

### Adding New Test Files
1. Create test file: `test_new_feature.cpp`
2. Add to appropriate `CMakeLists.txt`:
```cmake
add_executable(${_TEST_NAME}_tests 
    ${_TEST_NAME}_tests.cpp
    test_existing_feature.cpp
    test_new_feature.cpp  # Add here
)
```

```cmake
# Basic test discovery
catch_discover_tests(${_TEST_NAME}_tests TEST_PREFIX "${_TEST_NAME}: ")

# Advanced test discovery with customization
catch_discover_tests(${_TEST_NAME}_tests
    TEST_PREFIX "${_TEST_NAME}: "
    TEST_SUFFIX " (auto)"
    WORKING_DIRECTORY ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}
    EXTRA_ARGS --order rand --warn NoAssertions
    PROPERTIES

    SHARD_COUNT 4
    TEST_PREFIX "${_TEST_NAME}_shard: "
)
```

```cmake
# Feature-dependent tests
if (TARGET OpenVDB::openvdb)
    target_sources(${_TEST_NAME}_tests PRIVATE test_hollowing.cpp)
endif()

# Platform-specific tests
if(WIN32)
    target_sources(${_TEST_NAME}_tests PRIVATE test_windows_specific.cpp)
elseif(UNIX)
    target_sources(${_TEST_NAME}_tests PRIVATE test_unix_specific.cpp)
endif()

endif()

# Fast compile mode for development

    target_compile_definitions(${_TEST_NAME}_tests PRIVATE CATCH_CONFIG_FAST_COMPILE)
endif()
```

## Known Issues and Workarounds

### Platform-Specific Issues
```cpp
// MinGW/CygWin slow linking workaround
// Use: -fuse-ld=lld flag to speed up linking significantly

// Visual Studio 2017 raw string literal bug
#define CATCH_CONFIG_DISABLE_STRINGIFICATION
// This disables expression stringification but works around the compiler bug

// Visual Studio 2022 spaceship operator issue
// REQUIRE((a <=> b) == 0);  // May not compile with MSVC
// Workaround: use clang-cl or avoid spaceship in assertions

// QNX/VxWorks C stdlib issues
#include <cfoo>           // Use C++ headers
std::foo_function();     // Always call qualified
// NOT: #include <foo.h> and foo_function();
```

### Catch2 v3 Features Available
```cpp
// OrcaSlicer is on Catch2 v3.11.0 - all of these ARE available:

// - Sections can still be re-run if a later section fails (unchanged from v2)
```

1. **1:1 correspondence**: One test binary per library/module
2. **Hidden tests**: Use `[.]` or `[!benchmark]` tags for tests that shouldn't run by default

content.thinking:
I'm planning the page structure and starting to define the TypeScript interfaces for catalog settings and presets, laying out the data shapes needed for the component design.

I'm adding logic to clear the catalog when the session ID changes between state/context updates, keeping it tied to the current workspace session. Then I'm sketching the AllSettings component's props and scope state, where scope follows the current object selection and reverts to project-level when selection changes, plus a header component with back and collapse buttons.

Writing header and body markup...

For the plate and object scopes I'm adding summary components plus their own grouped settings sections. For project scope, I'm ordering groups as Quality, Strength, Speed, Support, Multimaterial, Others, then Filament and Printer, with each group collapsible via a header showing a chevron, name, and summary. I'm working out the default collapse behavior—leaning toward all groups closed by default, with search and the Changed filter auto-expanding groups that contain matches or changes.

I'm deciding that the first group plus any group with changes should open by default, since collapsing everything leaves the panel looking empty. For the summary text on each group header, I need to stick to counts like "N changed" or "from the preset" rather than naming specific settings, since the acceptance test forbids referencing setting keys anywhere except the extruder field—so I can't describe things like "0.20 mm layers" or "tree, build plate only" in the summary.

Within each group, rows get sub-grouped by Orca's metadata grouping, with each row showing the label and value, bolding changed values and adding a "Preset: X" line plus noting any object-level overrides elsewhere on the plate. I'm also planning search behavior—matching rows by label or key across all groups, auto-opening groups that have matches when a query is typed.

For the Changed filter, I'm deciding that object scope treats everything as "changed" since objects only have their own settings, so the filter becomes a no-op there, similarly for plate scope. For the Filament group with a single slot, I'm sub-grouping rows by filament page (Filament, Cooling, Setting Overrides, Advanced) and showing inherited values with a muted "printer" label and explanatory note.

For 2-3 slots, I'm laying out columns per slot with swatches and material names in the header, then rows sharing the union of keys from slot 1, with inherited cells shown muted as "printer" and overridden cells bolded with a short note like "Slot 3 overrides the printer's 0.8 mm."

For bed temperature rows, I'll check if the row's key matches the active plate's bedTempKey and if so append the bed type to the label, leaving other plate-temp rows unchanged. For 4+ slots, I'm adding a Select control above the rows to choose a single slot to display.

For object scope, I'm composing a summary sentence like "{name} uses the project's settings, except in N regions," grouping overrides by target — the whole object or individual named volumes.

I'm simplifying the override description logic: counting distinct volume targets as "regions" and reporting them by name, plus a separate count of settings overridden on the whole object itself, rather than trying to cleverly pluralize by type. Now I'm moving to the groups rendering — for each override with a settable key, finding its corresponding process row to determine which page group it belongs to.

For artifact-type overrides (no key, like support blockers), I'll skip action buttons entirely since read-only display was chosen, showing just the kind label, value, and a tag plus a note indicating the affected target. I'm mapping artifact kinds to groups: support-related ones go under Support, while seam/color/fuzzy-skin/variable-layer-height types get grouped under Others or Quality.

Groups with no overrides at all should still show a header but labeled "same as project," non-interactive with no chevron since there's nothing to expand. For object-scope overrides touching filament or printer settings, I'll show entries like filament slot and preset name, similar to the old page design.

For the plate scope, I need to handle the summary line noting the plate inherits project settings plus its own override count, then list the plate's own settings under a "Plate" group — though I'm unsure whether to show the project's original value as a note since some plate-level keys like print_sequence aren't in the catalogs the same way, so I'll just label them "Set on this plate." Below that, I'll list the objects on the plate, each showing either their own setting count or "same as project," clickable to jump into that object's scope.

For the presets box in project scope, I'm formatting the printer line as the printer name plus nozzle size(s), and starting on the filament row with a color swatch per slot.

For the select component, I'm considering giving ActionMenu a new `trigger="select"` prop with an `appearance` option mapping to a select-style class so the menu opens below, left-aligned and full width, as a minimal addition to ChatNavigation.tsx. I also need to handle loading states: showing a "Reading settings…" placeholder when the catalog is null, an unsupported-printer message when catalog.available is false, and keeping the old catalog visible without an indicator while a stale revision triggers a re-request.

For styling, rather than reusing the setup-screen-specific segmented control classes, I'll create generic `.jp-segmented`/`.jp-segment` and `.jp-select` classes with the same visual recipe, scoped to the settings panel, and add corresponding entries to the styles test recipes. I'm also verifying that the needed icon classes like chevron-down/left/right/up, search, and check already exist, and checking for a grid icon too.

Now I'm turning to App.tsx: I need to swap the 'setupDetails' view type for 'allSettings', add a `settingsCatalog` state field, and wire an effect that requests the settings catalog when entering that view (or when context revision changes), gracefully skipping if the host doesn't support it. In the render logic I'm adding a branch to show the AllSettings component with live catalog and historical context, treating historical chats as live-settings-only with some kind of note since the catalog isn't persisted per saved chat.

I'm reconsidering that approach — instead of maintaining two separate rendering paths for historical vs live data, I'll build a single pseudo-catalog from the historical context's presetDeltas and appliedSetup.localOverrides, so both cases flow through one rendering path with the "Changed" filter forced on and "All" disabled. That feels like the cleaner solution, so I'll go with `catalogFromContext(context)`.

Then I'm moving on to shell_harness.cpp changes involving two clicks...

I also need to account for similar join patterns like "Bed temperature | Bed temperature" and "Retraction | Retraction Length" on the filament and printer pages, and adjust the harness to click the Changed segment rather than assume it's default. For the hand-edit count check, I'm working through how the "4 changes from the preset" count should include the filament bed-temperature change and the printer retraction change alongside the process ones.

I don't know the exact breakdown, so instead of hardcoding the split I'll have the ready script compute the count directly by counting the changed-row elements in the DOM and writing that count into the draft text, so the harness check can verify against the real data rather than a guess.

With that settled, I'm ready to start implementing: protocol.ts, store.ts, tokens.ts, ChatNavigation variant selection, CSS and styles tests, then AllSettings.tsx, App.tsx, the test suite, the SetupCard link, removing SetupPage, and finally the harness.
